title: Buick Doesn’t Sell Sedans in the U.S., But China Will Get the Sleek New Electra GS Plug-In Hybrid - Car and Driver
content: Designed for the Chinese market, the Electra GS looks significantly different than the concept shown last year, with sharp, C-shaped LED headlights. While there are reports of a new sedan on the horizon, Buick’s lineup in the United States currently only consists of SUVs. But over in China, Buick offers a healthy arsenal of sedans, from the compact Verano to the larger LaCrosse. Now Buick is about to introduce a new electrified sedan called the Electra GS, and the first images of the new car have been leaked via China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The MIIT periodically publishes information on upcoming automotive products, and the official filing is the first time we’ve seen the final production design for the Electra GS, which was first previewed by a concept in 2025. Confusingly, Buick already offers a sedan called the Electra L7 in China, sold with electric and range-extender plug-in hybrid powertrains, but the new Electra GS seems poised to be a less potent and more affordable option. The new Electra GS is a bit smaller than the Electra L7, measuring 196.0 inches from nose to tail, just over two inches shy of the L7. The GS is also 1.5 inches narrower and has a 5.3-inch shorter wheelbase than the L7. Under the hood, the Electra GS will employ a plug-in hybrid setup that uses either a 97-hp naturally aspirated 1.5-liter inline-four or a turbocharged 1.5-liter making 154 hp. The gas engines are paired with an electric motor producing 221 horsepower, which feeds off a lithium iron phosphate battery. Stylistically, the production Electra GS is a significant departure from the concept, with a more traditional sedan shape than the concept’s taller, hatchback look. The front end has thin headlights that wrap around a trim piece that stretches across the front and can be either body colored or finished in silver. The Electra GS has a fastback roofline and smooth surfacing, while the taillights span the width of the vehicle before curving inward. Overall, the Electra GS looks smart and modern, and Buick will hope that the GS can help reverse its sales slide in China. The Electra GS won’t be coming to the U.S., but it could give a sense of Buick’s future styling direction that could appear on the rumored gas-powered sedan expected to arrive in the next couple of years. Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan. 2027 Chevrolet Trax Pricing Reveals $2000 Increase Hyundai Recalls 38K Cars Over Airbags and Seatbelts We may earn a commission for purchases made through our links.

title: How Aaru Uses Advanced AI Simulations to Predict Human Behavior - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Aaru, a two-and-a-half-year-old startup valued at $1 billion, is redefining market research and consumer intelligence by deploying multi-agent AI simulations to predict how humans will make decisions. Cam Fink, co-founder and CEO, and Ned Koh, co-founder and president, discuss Aaru's founding story and how advanced behavioral simulation overcomes the limitations of traditional consumer polling. In this conversation with Goldman Sachs Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti, they also explore the real-world enterprise applications of such predictive simulations across retail, financial services, and utilities, which are driving Aaru's rapid rise. Cam Fink:    We help you understand the composition of any population on the globe, and what decisions they make. What marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what subway lines they're going to ride. Ned Koh:      Our model is able to process how humans are able to think. Marco Argenti:      Welcome to Talks at GS. And also welcome to Ned and Cam from Aaru. Nowadays with AI almost like anything is possible, including being 19 and then, you know, having a $1 billion valuation startup, which is pretty incredible. So, since then, Aaru has become one of the most closely watched companies in the research and intelligence space. Thank you for being here. Cam Fink:    Thank you, Marco, for hosting us. We're really glad to have the opportunity today to talk a bit more about what we do. Marco Argenti:      The first question I'm going to ask you is, when was the first time you kind of realized that AI was something big? Cam Fink:    So, it's interesting you ask this because the ChatGPT moment was right in our senior year of high school. So, I remember, you know, having worked in the NLP space, in the computer vision space, where Ned and I were researchers before ChatGPT was released. You could tell that like AI was gaining a lot of capabilities very quickly. But it wasn't until it became actually productized into something consumers could use that all of a sudden it felt like not only was AI going to gain capabilities, but actually that it would create serious change in how people work on, you know, ideas, on products. But even still, like I remember the most enterprising students were already using AI to evaluate their answers to papers or come up with new ideas or test new things. And if you were even more enterprising before that, you would have been using the GPT-3 API to try and finish papers. So, you know, I think that was truly the moment that it became clear AI was going to be inevitable. Marco Argenti:      Was there another ah-ha moment recently? Because, you know, right now it feels like things are changing so fast. What's another inflection point that you've seen? Ned Koh:      The tools are incredibly powerful for being used for incredibly rudimentary application: note taking, you know, or summarization as like the key use cases or demonstrations of like how this can help you. And I still think in many businesses it is. It's easy to get behind. There's not really any friction to adopting those technologies. And so, I think that the larger change is this wave of product-first AI businesses. You saw that in health care. You saw that in, you know, financial services and beyond. But I think it was when it went beyond just those into more complex applications, for sure. Marco Argenti:      So, rolling back, like, kind of two basics. If you're in front of a CEO that doesn't know what Aaru is and you have a few seconds to explain, what would you say to them? What's your pitch? Like you're 30 second pitch. Cam Fink:    We predict human behavior. So, we help you understand the composition of any population on the globe and what decisions they make. We can help you understand how U.S. household purchase decision makers are going to purchase products, what marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what music they're going to stream, what subway lines they're going to ride. That's really the core of what we do: predicting behavior to make better business decisions. Marco Argenti:      And I think we met maybe two years ago for the first time. So, really early on. So, what have you learned in terms of sort of what kinds of decisions is AI really good at predicting and what others are not that good? Ned Koh:      Yeah, I think the first place that you look when you define what good means is understanding like the relative for how people make those decisions today. Right? So, let's take something that's like very simple - product launches. So, you have someone who's going in front of a survey, you're asking people questions. It's easy to benchmark. And that's a very interesting market. Product innovation is massive for us. But when you think about like use cases and how that's kind of diverged across the board, the most relevant ones for us and where we offer the most amount of value, of course, are places where you may not traditionally have data. Right? And so, that may exist in a population who doesn't respond to surveys. The example I like to give is like everybody in this room is wearing a shirt. Did anyone tell someone how much they were willing to pay for it? Probably not. Right? But then you get into like other categories. Right. You know this answer better than I do. But you know, there are four industries that make up about like 15% of the GDP of the U.S. Airlines, telecom, utilities, insurance. What are the times that matter to those companies about their behavior? When do you remember who your cell provider is? When your cell service goes out. When do you remember that you pay bills to Con Ed? When your power goes out. When do you remember that you fly a specific airline versus another? When your flight gets delayed. Right? And so, on and so forth. When do you remember who your insurance is? When you crash a car. And so, those businesses, despite being massive, the most important place and time for them to understand the behavior of their customers is somewhere where it's fundamentally impossible to get inside their head inside that moment. Right? And so, the most interesting use cases to us have always been those areas that have the most challenging to reach groups. The time frames of traditional research, it can take weeks and weeks or months to get people in a room and ask them questions or show them a product. You don't have the ability to do that. Right? So, things that are compressed in timeline are the use cases that are most relevant for simulation because human insight just doesn't reach that same level. Marco Argenti:      But why can't you just ask ChatGPT? Cam Fink:    Language models themselves alone can't understand human behavior with the depth and the capability that is required to actually allow a business to trust their decisions. There are a lot of startups out there now doing what you might call synthetic personas. That's sort of like the last generation of the technology we build. They can be useful. Those startups can help you get like a really quick read on marketing copy. But if you want a decision that you can trust, you need something that's grounded in real world outcomes. And that's where someone like Aaru would come in. Everything we do is AI. Right? So, what underpins our capabilities to predict human behavior are models. Models that we train. Models that leverage LLMs but aren't LLMs alone. But through fusing kind of LLMs with statistical models and traditional mathematical models, we're able to be far more accurate and take advantage of all of LLMs’ advantages without falling into those kind of gaps with LLMs and predicting behavior. Marco Argenti:      And how do you verify the accuracy and the results? I mean, what is what's ground truth for you guys? Ned Koh:      At the end of the day, if you're trying to predict and make a decision better, what you should be aiming for is a better business outcome. That was very first principle to us, right? You want to benchmark it to the sales result, to the product selling better or selling worse or the limited time offer not flying off the shelves like you wanted it to. The way that we've been able to grow our business so quickly is by making sure that people walk out of a pilot with us and don't just say, "Yes, we came to a decision faster," but rather we came to a decision better than we otherwise would have. Marco Argenti:      So, let's actually kind of bring it to life a little bit with some examples. What does the client actually get? Give us some examples of that. Cam Fink:    So, we do a lot of work with CPG companies. We do a lot of work with retail, beauty, apparel, kind of like anything that touches a consumer brand. And every kind of business ultimately sells a product. But for consumer brands, it's typically really linear. You can hold the product in your hand, right? A canned beverage, a carton of milk, whatever it might be. So, we do a lot of product innovation work where we'll go work with, you know, a canned sparkling water company, for example. And that sparkling water company will come to us and say, "Hey, we've built this great business around this one core product. What is our next new product line, right? Is it still hydration? Is it a shelf-stable dairy product? Is it an energy drink? Is it--," you know, all of these things. And we can use Aaru to do everything from the very core conceptual stage of what is the next frontier, right, all the way into figuring out who exactly is the purchasing audience. Then into the product concept itself specifically. So, say we pick out that it's an energy drink. We figure out who the energy drink purchaser is going to be from this brand. And then we figure out, okay, what flavors of energy drink do we want to put out in the world? And then we can do everything from getting as niche as optimizing the caffeine content to helping figure out the right pack size and carry that entire product innovation cycle from start to finish in just a few weeks. And one of our clients we worked with, their product innovation cycle traditionally was nine months long, right? That's actually pretty quick for the CPG industry. A lot of the big global companies might be taking 12 months, 18 months, to go from product idea or, you know, new market entrant to ready for manufacturing. We managed to squeeze it down into eight weeks. That was a really, really, really powerful case study. And now the product ended up hitting the shelves earlier this year. And they saw more success than they had with any of their previous product launches before. Marco Argenti:      And if I remember, that you guys can decide the size of the core. Tell us a little bit about that spectrum. Cam Fink:    Yeah, we don't go down to individual-by-individual level, right? We're never processing PII or any kind of individual data. So, we can't recreate Tom Smith from Iowa or Cameron Fink from New York City, right? We can get down to audiences that in the real world might only be a couple hundred people. I remember at one point doing hospitals that have to purchase this third-party risk management software. You're probably talking only a few hundred to low thousands of people nationwide. And yet we were still able to recreate that audience. And for the company that we did do that study for, they saw a massive impact from the work we could do together. So, we're getting really niche. We can talk about very small groups of buyers or social media influencers or Gen Z in one particular city metro. And then we can go as wide as US household purchase decision-makers or British residents or, you know, even residents of the EU if you want it. Marco Argenti:      And where do you get your data? Cam Fink:    I mean, it's a massive wealth of data sources, right? So, when we talk about how we leverage that data, we have audience data and we have behavioral outcomes data. On the audience data component, that's what helps us understand who actually exists inside of a population. So, when you come to me and you say, "Hey, I want to talk to ultra high net worth individuals in, you know, the United States and Canada," we can actually tell you what the distribution of that population looks like. And then we have behavioral outcome data. That helps us figure out what decisions are they going to make. So, that would, you know, be for each of these given value propositions, how will UHMW individuals react to them? Now, when it comes to where that data actually comes from, you can think about three different buckets for each of the data sources that we leverage. The first would be publicly accessible data. We're leveraging tons of things like the census, academic research where there's license to train on top of it, you know, anything else available publicly that our model is able to use. Then there's a lot of data we purchase. So, we buy data from everyone from credit card, you know, purchase history data providers to receipts, there are music streams, social media data. And then I would say really the final component is proprietary partnerships that we leverage. So, we do a lot of work with organizations that wouldn't fit the shape of traditional customers of ours but still want access to the impact of our software. We have done data sharing through those sorts of engagements before that's been incredibly powerful for what we do too. Marco Argenti:      How do you make your clients comfortable that they can share their most valuable data? Cam Fink:    Every client is sandboxed entirely. We're SOC 2 compliant. I didn't expect that I'd be saying that up on stage. But just in case anyone was worried, we have any InfoSec people in the room, we are SOC 2 compliant. We have all the compliance certifications we can. Most importantly, we do not train on customer data. And all of our clients are sandboxed. So, we actually end up being trusted as one of the most secure places to store, you know, that data because you would never be able to leverage a traditional research provider for anything sensitive. Right? You wouldn't want to go survey people and then someone takes a screenshot and says, "Hey, you know, my favorite brand was polling me about this on the internet." Instead, when you're leveraging our software, it's kept entirely secure to, you know, the model that we train. Marco Argenti:      You just said the models that we train. So, has your attitude and approach shifted over the years with regards to kind of using your own models versus using frontier models versus using quasi frontier open-source models? Cam Fink:    Yeah, our approach has definitely changed. I mean, when we started the business, we were definitely more in this realm of like, hey, can you take an LLM and train it on top of survey results? We found some of our own issues with that, right? Historically, we found it wasn't extensible. And that's what really led us to the next generation of our technology. So, those are all the models that we built ourselves. And that was really the big leap forward in terms of how our technology was able to reach the accuracy level that it is today. And so, we've been on, you know, all of our own models ever since that point in time. LLMs help us write analysis. They help us do tons of tasks as part of the simulation pipeline. But LLMs aren't driving the fundamental underlying prediction and behavior themselves. Now, when it comes to the LLMs we integrate, we use tons of different providers. We default to whatever is the best provider for each task that we have to do. Marco Argenti:      Which could be, you know, somehow maybe filtering all the data or explaining or prompt interpretation. But then the actual prediction machine or the simulation machine is your own. And that's your secret sauce. Ned Koh:      That is the secret sauce. Every single economist in the history of like behavioral science and everything else that you can go into has dreamed to be able to build a model off of something that's based on outcomes. You want to be able to remove as much bias as possible. Right? And so, not always is the magic and the data exclusively. It's much more in how our model is able to process things that are in many ways useless by their own right into something that can become a holistic view of how humans are able to think. Marco Argenti:      If every customer is protected and everything, how do you evolve the model? Cam Fink:    We're integrating new data sources all the time, right? So, the data that we have alone is enough that we are able to go out and make tons of valuable predictions. We can generate a lot of insight without having to integrate client data. Integrating client data for us is the key to unlock, you know, much deeper capabilities and integrations, both in terms of, you know, the simulation component and also in terms of how simulation results end up getting used. Marco Argenti:      I get that. But within, let's say, client engagement though, let's say we use it in private wealth in GS and then we want to kind of continue to learn, so do you allow your clients to continuously learn on the model that you provide and that stays theirs? Cam Fink:    It's actually interesting. A huge part of what we're talking about now is this idea of compounding intelligence. One of the biggest issues that our clients feel, one of their biggest pains, is this idea that traditional insight is very static, right? You run one survey, you run another survey, maybe you run a quarterly brand tracker, but it's not like those survey results are propelling forth the next survey that you run. And when you think about simulation, what's really incredible about the difference with our platform is that it's not just the power to like access more accurate, faster results. Our simulations can also contain the insights from all the simulations before it. And what that means is that it actually builds and compounds in value over time. You can imagine someone using our platform at the end of running nine projects about studying the Gen Z audience together, could come to us and say, "What are the insights, you know, we didn't even know we had about the Gen Z audience?" And that can go into helping build the next product that people might be interested in. So, a big focus for us is that compounding intelligence piece. Marco Argenti:      Are you guys mostly focused on the US, or do you have a lot of international customers? Cam Fink:    Yeah, we're a totally global business in terms of what we support. So, when you think about the range of Aaru today, it's over 130 countries across the globe. All of the EU, all of North America, much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, you know, and beyond. In the future, we are actually planning international expansion starting soon. But today, the bulk of our customers are based in North America. Marco Argenti:      And so, on that note, so do you think you need to tune sort of your models by culture and by countries? Ned Koh:      I think one of the best markets that is super relevant for a lot of the biggest enterprises that we work with today is expansion into Germany is really interesting, right? I've seen this across customers of ours in consumer electronics. I've seen this across customers of ours in financial services, right? Like it really goes across so many areas. The amount of safety regulations that people care about in like South Florida versus in, you know, Central Germany are vastly different. I can tell you that, right? Like the reality is, you know, you talk about why do we train models within this time when you're actually in runtime? Why do we keep them updated? These sorts of elements. The news, the way they digest social media, the things that changed their environment is what we like to call it within a given sim. Absolutely do. The context of how you and I make decisions on today versus tomorrow, absolutely do change. Does my race change? No, that's not the most important part to measure. So, we absolutely have to do that and have to do it on a hyper localized basis. Marco Argenti:      What's your biggest bottleneck at this point? Cam Fink:    100% hiring. Like it's the best people in the world is the number one thing you need for any fast-growing business. And so, when we think about what is going to-- has defined the last six months, going to define the next six months, next six years of Aaru, it's all going to be about working with the best people in the world. Marco Argenti:      And what kind of people are you looking for? Cam Fink: The first thing that we evaluate for is raw capability. We do look for people who are the best in the world at something. Right? People who are truly excellent at the craft or at their craft, so to speak, and represent the pinnacle of understanding knowledge capability in a given area. That's something that every person wants. Right? I'm sure Goldman wants people who are the best in their craft as well. We also look for people who are really high slope. So, even if you're not the absolute best in the world at something today, do you have the potential to be that in the future? Can you learn quickly? Can you adapt is something that's really important to us as well. And then finally, we look for people who are real collaborators. Every time someone joins our team, it's not just about whether or not they themselves are a really, really brilliant individual. Tons of people who are super smart and, you know, would be lucky to work at any incredible business on the globe. We spend a lot of time focusing on who is exactly right for Aaru and the people who have much to teach our team, much to teach myself, but we also have much to teach them and they can be, you know, leverage, exponential or multiplicative leverage to the people around them. Ned Koh:      Most of our research team, right, you'll have people who are pure math backgrounds. You'll have people who have done Alzheimer's and dementia research, right, who are able to tie in these really interesting areas. On the other side, we've recently brought on the head of research and data science from Qualtrics, who was there for over 13 years. Right? It's like you need some of those incredibly experienced perspectives to understand how to solve these problems. But you also need very fresh ones to think outside of the box to be able to do it as well. It's all about a combination and a balance. Cam Fink:    I think what we believed was true when we started this business is still true for the most part. Right? Like, we've always believed in being open communicators. We've always believed internally in, you know, the power of learning from each other, the power of collaboration. I think those are all important things. We've always believed in wanting people who are excellent at their craft. When we started to think about it, it's that as a growing business, it's actually time to write that down for the first time and distill it into the things that matter most for us. And that is what led us to kind of starting to think more about culture and principles in the last few weeks than we had previously. Ned Koh:      To that point, a really interesting thing that we've been discussing, especially with some of the larger implications of being able to model behavior, is this idea of like trustworthiness of a model. There's a very big difference between being worthy of trust and being a trustworthy company. And we certainly try to stay on the prior, right? We define that as being worthy of trust to the people who work next to you, right? That you're going to do an incredible job. It's being worthy of trust of your investors. It's being worthy of trust of your customers. It's being worthy of trust of the world that you're using the technology for the biggest impacts you can. Ned Koh:      Thank you so much for having us, Marco. Marco Argenti:      Was great. And good luck. Thank you so much. title: Emerging Market Credit Shows Resilience amid Energy Shock - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. When the Iran war triggered a surge in oil prices this year, many investors may have expected credit markets in the developing world to slide into a selloff. Instead, emerging market sovereign and corporate bonds weathered the shock with a newfound stability and solid performance for investors. The development is a key sign that emerging market credit is maturing into a resilient asset class, according to Anupam Damani, co-head and senior portfolio manager of emerging market debt at Goldman Sachs Asset Management. At the same time, investors are rethinking their approach to the market, which has trillions of dollars in outstanding debt. “Emerging market credit is now unrecognizable, and I mean that in a good way,” Damani says. “These bonds used to come with a crisis label, but this market is no longer monolithic. In my view, it has become a more diverse and resilient asset class, though risks remain.” To be sure, emerging market bonds run the gamut in terms of risk, and investors must be selective about what they trade in a marketplace with myriad issuers, she adds. We spoke with Damani about the changing dynamics in the asset class, including the growth of emerging market corporate bonds and a less binding US dollar. For a long time, emerging market credit (EM credit) was considered a risk-on or a risk-off trade. Now, there are what we like to call more dispersed opportunity sets, or more names to choose from. We believe this reflects fundamental improvements that may have reduced binary tail risk—the all-or-nothing quality that used to define EM credit.  In our view, this has become an asset class where credit selection really matters. The market has matured. In the sovereign space, for example, you’ll see deep local-currency markets with stronger reserve buffers. This means more liquidity. There are also more credible inflation-policy frameworks and deeper domestic investor bases. It is, and this trend is unfolding across regions, from Asia to Latin America, Eastern Europe, and Africa. I believe these changes have anchored the market very differently than in the past. There used to be only a few countries in the EM sovereign space. Now, there are more than 80 countries offering a far wider range of potential opportunities. Well, it’s been an evolution. There are countries that are developing strong institutions, and there are always going to be a few countries that are moving backward. This isn’t a linear progression across the asset class. But on an aggregate level, I think there has been a greater focus on fiscal orthodoxy and monetary orthodoxy. And to see the results, look at how many major emerging markets are running close to their inflation targets, with significant GDP growth, even in the face of the energy supply shock this year. When you look at developed markets, investors are struggling to see the same kind of discipline. Indeed, investors are increasingly demanding a higher risk premium to own some developed market assets. In my view, what’s interesting is that in emerging markets, there has always been a demand for higher risk premiums because of perceived notions around governance and weakness in policy frameworks. I think this has moved quite a bit. EM credit used to be largely a sovereign-only market. Today, we have a rapidly evolving market for corporates. And issuers are companies with footprints that extend beyond their borders—they are globally competitive, industry leaders that deal in hard currency. They are supported by local markets, with domestic consumer investor bases that have become larger and deeper in recent years. In fixed income, we believe emerging market corporates have historically offered attractive Sharpe ratios, or risk-adjusted performance, relative to many other sectors. In our view, this reflects the bonds' strong resilience, credit quality, and lower duration. Yes. The US dollar constraint is less binding than it used to be in previous cycles. In the 1990s, for instance, issuance was overwhelmingly dollar-driven, so when the dollar appreciated massively, your payment capacity was reduced as the local currency cost of servicing the debt rose. Now that effect is decreasing with the growth of local-currency sovereign debt markets. Emerging market countries are also issuing more debt in euros and renminbi. We believe this is an underappreciated development in the EM credit story. There used to be a transparency discount for investors because data on issuers was considered too opaque. If you look at the investable universe in EM corporates today, disclosure looks much closer to what we see in developed markets. There is standardized reporting of data under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) or IFRS-aligned frameworks. This improves comparability across regions and sectors, which we didn’t have in the past. Balance sheet transparency is also far stronger. Issuers have also improved communications with investors—quarterly reporting, presentations, earnings calls, roadshows—just as we see in developed markets. When there are negative developments in a country or broader industry, those communications tend to pick up. You didn’t see this type of healthy dialogue between issuers and investors in the past. It’s a pertinent question for the asset class. In our view, what’s important is the convergence around institutional frameworks, orthodox policies on inflation, and stronger fiscal reserve positions. These developments may have increased the ability of emerging markets to better absorb these types of shocks. In this cycle, for example, we have not seen uniform stress across the market but rather a dispersion across credits. This is an important point. If you look at what’s happening in the Middle East, we have oil prices shooting up. In emerging market credit, we have energy exporters and importers, right?  This creates greater differentiation across issuers in the marketplace rather than the broad-based selloffs seen in some prior EM crises. And it shows that over the years, many developing economies have learned from their mistakes and tried to make changes that make them more resilient. So returns are increasingly driven by fundamentals and valuations, and that is a very different proposition from simply owning what we used to call the EM beta trade. title: Princeton to honor Nobel laureates Frances Arnold ’79 and Mary Brunkow GS ’91 at Alumni Day 2027 - The Daily Princetonian
content: Princeton’s top alumni honors will go to Nobel laureates Frances Arnold ’79, an engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology, and Mary Brunkow GS ’91, a distinguished investigator at Seattle’s Institute for Systems Biology. Arnold will receive the Woodrow Wilson Award while Brunkow will be awarded the James Madison Medal at Alumni Day on Feb. 20, 2027. The Woodrow Wilson Award was established in 1956 and is named after Woodrow Wilson, Class of 1879, who served as Princeton’s president before becoming U.S. president. The award is given to an undergraduate alum whose work represents Wilson’s saying, “Princeton in the nation’s service.” The 2026 awardee was Smithsonian executive Kevin Gover ’78, and Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor ’76 won the award in 2014. Originally from Pittsburgh, Arnold studied mechanical and aerospace engineering at Princeton, graduating magna cum laude in 1979. Her father, William Howard Arnold GS ’55, was a nuclear physicist and Princeton alumnus. Arnold was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2018 for her research that pioneered the directed evolution of enzymes involving introducing random mutations to proteins over many generations to engineer ones with desired traits. The Arnold Lab at Caltech is centered on engineering biological systems through “directed evolution,” with applications in pharmaceuticals, consumer products, renewable fuels, and bioremediation. According to her Nobel Prize biography, Arnold was one of the few women in her mechanical and aerospace engineering classes at Princeton, and studied economics, foreign languages, and art history along with the math and physics required for engineering. Beginning in her junior year, Arnold studied at the Center for Energy and Environmental Studies, now known as the Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, with a focus on sustainable energy, influenced by the energy crisis of the 1970s and mentors at Princeton who believed that energy research could lead to positive societal change. Arnold is also an inventor with over 60 U.S. patents, co-founding the company Gevo, which produces biofuel from fermented plant materials, and Provivi, which creates alternatives to pesticides. Arnold did not provide comment in time for publication. The James Madison Medal, named for Princeton’s first graduate alumnus, is the highest honor a graduate alum can receive. It is awarded to alumni who have exhibited extraordinary public service, furthered graduate education, or had exceptional career success. Previous awardees have included Terence Tao GS ’96, Julia Wolfe GS ’12, and Robert Kahn GS ’64. The medal is not Brunkow’s first major honor, who won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2025, alongside immunologists Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi for their work in peripheral immune tolerance. Brunkow said the medal was “a real honor” in an interview with The Daily Princetonian. “I see the list of all the past awardees, and it’s pretty amazing to be part of that esteemed crowd of achievers.” Brunkow earned her Ph.D. in molecular biology from Princeton in 1991. Her doctoral adviser was Shirley M. Tilghman, who would go on to serve as Princeton’s 19th president. Beyond helping her develop a strong foundation in scientific methodology and science communication, Brunkow also credits Tilghman as “an amazing role model.” “There weren’t very many really senior-level women in research at that time,” Brunkow told the ‘Prince.’ “I was lucky at the time to be … working with somebody who really embodied what it takes to succeed in a really difficult role.” Brunkow currently works at the Institute for Systems Biology in Seattle, where she serves as a Distinguished Investigator in the Hood Lab. Her involvement in biology has changed considerably throughout her career, ranging from genomics to her Nobel Prize-winning research in immunology. Today, her work centers on systems biology. When asked about what draws her to the field, she cited the potential impact her research can have. “[It is] very satisfying and very exciting to me that the science has evolved a lot over the last few decades so that we really can think about making discoveries that will really impact how clinicians treat patients,” she told the ‘Prince.’ Both Brunkow and Arnold will receive their awards on campus in the Spring. title: China's Buick Electra GS Is A Stylish Hybrid America Can't Have - CarScoops
content: GM could definitely use plug-in hybrid sedan in its U.S. lineup Buick hasn't offered a sedan in the U.S. since sales of the Regal ended in 2020. But it's a totally different story in China, where SUV haters can choose from multiple low-riding four-door cars, including the handsome, electrified Electra L7. Now, Buick's Chinese division is gearing up to launch its Electra GS little brother, and you have to wonder if America is missing out. Details of the Electra GS were revealed by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology filings ahead of the official debut, and they tell us the production car has changed quite a bit since GM showed the Electra GS concept (below) at the Shanghai Auto Show in 2025. The LED headlights have been inverted, and the Buick badge moved from the hood to a front facia that features less body-color plastic. The concept was incredibly handsome, but maybe looked a little too much like a Tesla Model 3 around the front. The production car looks less like a Tesla, but sacrifices some eye candy points. An imminent ban on pop-out door handles in China meant the concept's had to go, and though the fastback profile is carried across, the show car's traditional sedan trunk has made way for a more practical hatch. The taillights are also new, and so is the "Buick" lettering spelled out at the rear of the car. Another genuinely massive change is the productions GS's massive reduction in scale. MIIT data shows it's 196.1 inches (4,980 mm) long, but the concept (pictured above) was a huge 208.7 inches (5,300 mm). Same thing with wheelbase. The concept's axles were 126 inches (3,200 mm) apart, but the production GS wheelbase measures 112.8 inches (2,865 mm), making the finished car similar in size to a Toyota Crown, rather than a Mercedes S-Class. The biggest switch of all, though, takes place under the hood. GM didn't reveal much in the way of technical details about the concept, but it did confirm it was a fully electric car that rode on a dedicated EV platform, giving a totally flat floor. But, like Adam West's 1966 Batman jumping on the Batpoles inside Wayne Manor dressed in a comfy cardigan, and emerging inside the Batcave in full caped crusader garb 100 ft (31 m) down, the GS bound for dealers has arrived for duty as a plug-in hybrid. Base cars pair a 97 horsepower (98 PS) naturally aspirated 1.5-liter inline-4 with a 221 hp (224 PS) electric motor, but a more expensive variant swaps the NA gas motor for a turbocharged version of the same, making 154 hp (156 PS). We'll have wait for the full China debut to find out more about the GS, including whether the interior looks anything like the concept's (below). But don't pin your hopes on seeing that yoke steering wheel — we can already see a conventional steering wheel is present in the studio images of the exterior. Back in the U.S., GM's sales have been hurt by its lack of hybrid offerings. The automaker was so sure EVs would dominate the car market by the end of the decade that it didn't bother developing them, except for the Corvette E-Ray (now renamed Grand Sport X). Rival brands like Toyota and Hyundai hedged their bets, and made both, and are now reaping the rewards, while GM is rushing to catch up toward the end of the decade. Could the GS work here? Absolutely, but it's not likely. GM does import vehicles from China, including Chinese-built Buick Envision from China, although production of that model is due to shift to Kansas in 2028. Complicating matters is the fact that the GS is the result of a joint venture between GM and China's SAIC, and new restrictions on Chinese software that take effect with the 2027 model year would make it tricky to get this car compliant for the U.S. market, even if production was shifted to North America to avoid tariffs. Overall, we'd say don't hold your breath for this Buick.

title: Crazy Like Jeremy Fox: Birdie G’s Returns While The Restaurant at Edna Marks a New Chapter - Observer
content: What is it like to open two high-profile restaurants, in two different cities, in less than two weeks? For chef Jeremy Fox, it’s a crazy but surprisingly calming experience. By clicking submit, you agree to our terms of service and acknowledge we may use your information to send you emails, product samples, and promotions on this website and other properties. You can opt out anytime. Fox, a versatile chef who followed up his “On Vegetables” cookbook with his “On Meat” cookbook, has worked in the top tier of fine dining in California and also created comforting, nostalgic food that celebrates Americana and the Jewish-American diaspora. In Los Angeles, he’s long been a leader of seasonal, market-driven cuisine. But recently, it was unclear whether he would cook in a restaurant again. He closed Birdie G’s, a deeply personal restaurant named for his daughter and inspired by his grandmother’s home cooking, in Santa Monica at the end of 2025. The closure, one of many in L.A. spurred by an economic downturn, left Fox unmoored. But now Birdie G’s is back, with an expanded repertoire, at a high-profile new location in Los Angeles. On October 26, Fox opened the new Birdie G’s inside the Fairmont Century Plaza hotel. Unlike the previous dinner-only Birdie G’s, the new restaurant serves breakfast, lunch and dinner. “It’s a muscle I’ve never used before,” Fox told Observer on opening night after we ate his fried-oyster-topped riff on Caesar salad, soul-warming matzo ball soup, “pickle chick” schnitzel and Flannery steak frites before indulging in a slice of jiggly rose petal pie. What added to the craziness is that Fox knew he would be in San Luis Obispo a few days later for friends-and-family service at The Restaurant at Edna. Fox and former Birdie G’s executive chef Matthew Schaler will open that vineyard restaurant, with a focus on local agriculture, on Thursday, November 5. The timing of restaurant openings is always unpredictable, and the original goal was to open Birdie G’s and The Restaurant at Edna months apart. “I will say that I planned to open both restaurants in the same week,” Fox joked this week when Observer asked him about his intense timeline. “That was the goal. I nailed it.” But the reality is, he is now the opposite of unmoored, and it’s a good feeling. “I’ve made no attempts to hide that I deal with anxiety,” Fox, who’s known for speaking freely about his mental health, tells Observer. “I spent much of this year pretty deep in anxiety because I didn’t have a place to go every day. I was used to having deadlines every day. I had to be ready for service every day. And my deadlines were all, like, eight months away. It was an anxiety of, like, ‘Am I achieving as much in my day as I should?’ … But as things ramped up in the last two-and-a-half months, I’ve actually been calmer. I’ve always been someone who, the more engaged I am, the more semi-overwhelmed I am, the calmer I am, and the more I’m able to block out the noise. As it’s gotten crazier, I’ve gotten calmer.” It helps, of course, that he’s got an arsenal of dishes and techniques that he’s honed for decades. At Birdie G’s, he’s put a Rancho Gordo yellow eye bean stew on the lunch menu. That stew originated at Manresa, when David Kinch asked Fox to help create a patio menu. Fox then served the stew at Ubuntu and Rustic Canyon. The stew “appears to have an ungodly amount of garlic,” Fox says. “The garlic has to be cooked a certain amount, or else it disappears or overpowers the stew. It’s a matter of toasting the rosemary, the chili flakes and the garlic and olive oil, but not to the point where the garlic takes on any color. But it does have to be cooked through.” Meanwhile, making Birdie G’s matzo ball soup, which is enriched with carrot miso, is a “regimented” process. Fox was influenced by both how his grandmother Gladys made matzo ball soup and how specific his wife, Rachael Sheridan, is about chicken broth when she makes matzo ball soup. Birdie G’s is about Fox’s family and his desire to make everyday food. The Restaurant at Edna, with its focus on seasonal cooking and regional wines, is about using a different kind of muscle, one that Fox has called upon a lot in his career. “It’s designed for the things I’m good at,” Fox says of the dinner-only, five-night-a-week restaurant. “There’s no concept to it. This is one of the ways I like to cook, where the menu changes constantly. It’s based on the buildability of the best local ingredients, prepared thoughtfully. Not fussy, though. The room begs itself to be a destination restaurant, but we really want to try to not fall into that. We want to be someplace where you can go every week, and there will be new things on the menu as well as things you remember that you had last time. And then dishes might be gone forever, or they might come back next year.” During friends-and-family dinners, Fox and Schaler got raves for dishes like cone cabbage stuffed with smoked bacon, ramps and an egg-yolk sauce; sweet potato and pumpkin pavé with brown butter sabayon, sage and truffles; and mushroom ravioli shaped like mushrooms and featuring fonduta made with Stepladder Moonstone cheese. There’s also the Edna salad, with a beet-based French dressing that Schaler impressed Fox with when he was applying to work at the original Birdie G’s. The Restaurant at Edna will serve local seafood like Petrale sole and California meat like Flannery beef. Fox is buying ingredients from nearby farms that previously supplied him in Los Angeles for more than a decade. He’s looking at shellfish from uni diver Stephanie Mutz. This is his wheelhouse. But life, as Fox has long known, is about different things being true at the same time. Fox and his family eat at Silver Lake’s Astro diner more than any other restaurant in Los Angeles. He very much wants Birdie G’s to be a comforting, unintimidating, everyday L.A. restaurant. “The restaurants that originally inspired me to want to be part of the restaurant business were Applebee’s, Chili’s, The Cheesecake Factory, those kinds of places,” Fox says. “I went to culinary school and followed the path of fine dining when, originally, all I wanted to do was have a place that people like to go eat.” “It’s accessible food,” he says. “It’s recognizable. The original Birdie G’s was a crowd-pleaser. People who came really loved it and connected with it. A lot of people would say they haven’t had anything like that since their grandmother cooked it.” But most grandmothers don’t do things like make a Caesar salad enhanced by “A.C.G.” powder with anchovies, capers and garlic that are cooked down in olive oil for more than a day and then strained and dehydrated. Fox thinks a lot about the two dramatically contrasting restaurants in the movie “Big Night” and how he finds them both compelling. “Birdie G’s, for me, was a way to kind of have one foot in both worlds, with the understated subtle cuisine and also the more over-the-top and accessible food while trying to be a little bit subversive,” he says. The food at Birdie G’s is delicious and fun and a little crazy. For Fox, there’s comfort in the craziness. We get it: you like to have control of your own internet experience. title: Text of Pope Leo's Nov. 4 general audience - Catholic Standard
content: The following is the full text of Pope Leo XIV’s general audience address given Nov. 4 at St. Peter’s Square. The Documents of the Second Vatican Council. IV. Constitution Gaudium et Spes. 8. Faith and social, political, and economic life Dear brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome! The social dimension is an integral part not only of human nature, but also of our faith in Christ Jesus, as the precious legacy we receive from the Incarnation of the Son of God. The Constitution Gaudium et Spes (GS) recalls this in Chapters III and IV of Part II, dedicated to economic and social life and to the life of the political community. In these areas too, the Christian faith offers criteria for discernment. The Council Fathers highlight, first of all, the threat to world peace deriving from the imbalances linked to an economic development that is neither equitable nor respectful of creation (cf. GS, 63). This is a far-sighted vision, which was unfortunately borne out towards the end of the last century and which we see even more clearly today. To correct this course, the Document warns, technical progress alone is not enough: “many reforms in the socioeconomic realm and a change of mentality and attitude are required of all” (ibid.). Therefore, Gaudium et Spes summarizes the Christian vision of economic development, which must always be at the service of humankind and under human control (cf. GS, 64–65). The concept of integral development is already clearly evident here, a concept which Saint Paul VI would later place at the heart of his Encyclical Populorum Progressio (1967). More relevant than ever are the appeals to commit to eliminating discrimination against the most vulnerable social groups and migrants (cf. GS, 66). The heart of the economy is work. Through it, one develops as a person, provides for family needs, expresses one’s own talent, participates in social life and builds a better world by collaborating in God’s creative work. Work must never be distorted to the detriment of people, the common good or creation. The real challenge is to offer everyone opportunities to make the most of their abilities: unemployment, exploitation and working conditions that endanger health and life itself are unacceptable (cf. GS, 67). Workers have the right and the duty to participate in decisions affecting their work, including through trade unions, resolving conflicts through dialogue and non-violent action (cf. GS, 68). In this context, the Council recalls one of the fundamental principles of social teaching, namely the universal destination of earthly goods (cf. GS, 69) and applies it to the financial sphere, stating that “whoever makes decisions concerning these investments and the planning of the economy – whether they be individuals or groups of public authorities – are bound … to recognize their serious obligation of watching, on the one hand, that provision be made for the necessities required for a decent life both of individuals and of the whole community and, on the other, of looking out for the future and of establishing a right balance between the needs of present-day consumption, both individual and collective, and the demands of investing for the generation to come” (GS, 70). Gaudium et Spes then goes on to discuss the political community, noting several positive developments in the contemporary era, above all the fact that “the present keener sense of human dignity has given rise in many parts of the world to attempts to bring about a politico-juridical order which will give better protection to the rights of the person in public life” (GS, 73). The political community exists for the sake of the common good, which consists of “the sum of those conditions of the social life whereby men, families and associations more adequately and readily may attain their own perfection” (GS, 74). The exercise of political authority must always be directed towards the common good, which must be structured and operate according to local and historical circumstances, but always with the good of the entire human family at heart (cf. ibid.). Gaudium et Spes reiterates that “the Church and the political community in their own fields are autonomous and independent from each other. Yet both, under different titles, are devoted to the personal and social vocation of the same men. The more that both foster sounder cooperation between themselves with due consideration for the circumstances of time and place, the more effective will their service be exercised for the good of all” (GS, 76). Dear friends, engaging in economic and political life in accordance with these criteria is a way of building peace. As Pope Francis recalled, “war is a failure of politics and of humanity, a shameful capitulation, a stinging defeat before the forces of evil” (Encyclical Letter Fratelli tutti, 261). On the contrary, politics that tends to the wounds of peoples and of those who suffer injustice offers grounds for hope for the future of humanity. For this reason, I encourage young people to follow the example of those men and women who have borne faithful witness in these fields. And I renew my call to Christian communities to revive formation in the social doctrine of the Church. I greet all the English-speaking pilgrims and visitors taking part in today’s Audience, especially those from England, Ireland, Denmark, Malta, the Netherlands, Norway, Nigeria, Australia, Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and the United States of America. In a particular way, I welcome the members of the National Conference of Vocation Directors for England and Wales. Upon all of you and your families, I invoke the joy and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ. God bless you! Pope Leo XIV smiles from the popemobile while riding around St. Peter’s Square at the Vatican before his weekly general audience Nov. 4, 2026. (CNS photo/Lola Gomez)

title: NBA Power Rankings: Summing up all 30 teams' starts - ESPN
content:
Just two weeks into the NBA season, storylines have been flipped as injuries and surprise surges reverberate around the league. The Philadelphia 76ers have dominated their opponents early -- and are having some fun in the process. Meanwhile, the reigning champion New York Knicks are attempting to claw themselves back into the top echelon after starting the season 0-3. It's in the West where things have started to heat up. The Oklahoma City Thunder and Minnesota Timberwolves are dealing with injuries to their stars, making way for players such as the Memphis Grizzlies' Ty Jerome to have an early impact in his team's standings. The Los Angeles Lakers' Luka Doncic is making an early MVP case and doesn't seem to be slowing down after scoring 42 and 45 points in his past two games. And the Portland Trail Blazers, sans Ja Morant as he deals with an injury, are showing that depth is what will set teams apart across the league. In our second iteration of Power Rankings since the season started, our NBA insiders assigned four words to describe each team's start to 2026-27, and break down why things are -- or are not -- working. Note: Team rankings are based on where members of our panel (ESPN's Jamal Collier, Michael C. Wright, Tim MacMahon, Dave McMenamin, Vincent Goodwill, Zach Kram, Ben Golliver, Kris Rhim and Anthony Slater) think teams belong. Jump to a team:
ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE
DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND
LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN
NO | NY | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX
POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS Next games: vs. MIN (Nov. 4), @ PHX (Nov. 7), vs. DEN (Nov. 9) VanVleet's impact is immeasurable. The Rockets navigated the choppy waters of Kevin Durant's first season nearly rudderless without floor general Fred VanVleet, who sustained a season-ending knee injury before the start of training camp. Now that he's back, Houston is a calmer, more organized team. VanVleet directs traffic, manipulates defenses to set up teammates for shots in their preferred spots and limits turnovers, catalyzing a Houston offense with the league's best rating (121.2). Wisely, the Rockets added ballhandling insurance with another veteran point guard in Marcus Smart, who can start in VanVleet's place when he sits the second night of back-to-backs. -- Michael C. Wright Next games: vs. PHI (Nov. 4), vs. LAL (Nov. 8), vs. WAS (Nov. 9) 3-pointers have improved. The Pistons have developed a reputation for stifling defense and it hasn't changed, being first in points per game against and defensive rating. What has seemed to improve early is their 3-point shooting. Cade Cunningham is carrying over his playoff 3-point shooting with a career-high 37%, and Kevin Huerter, who struggled after coming from Chicago at midseason, is at a more-than-respectable clip of 38.5% (he shot 29% in 25 games last season). Duncan Robinson is No. 4 in makes, and the team collectively has risen to No. 6 in percentage (38.1). Their season high in triples in a game in 2025-26 was 18, a mark they've matched twice in the first two weeks. -- Vince Goodwill Next games: @ DET (Nov. 4), @ CLE (Nov. 6), @ CHI (Nov. 8), vs. BOS (Nov. 10) The Tyrese Maxey Show.  Maxey has been Philly's best player while being on a team with two former MVPs, LeBron James and Joel Embiid, and a Finals MVP in Jaylen Brown. The 25-year-old leads the Sixers in scoring and has buoyed them late in games this season with explosive fourth quarters that have kept them winning. He leads the NBA in fourth-quarter scoring (11.0). "I just think he now feels -- like in a nonarrogant and even a humble way -- he knows he's really, really good," coach Nick Nurse said of Maxey. "And I'm not sure that was always the case." -- Kris Rhim Next games: vs. MIL (Nov. 4), @ CHA (Nov. 6), @ MIL (Nov. 8), @ PHI (Nov. 10) They'll be just fine. The Celtics traded All-NBA forward Brown fresh off his best season for 36-year-old Paul George this offseason, a return that came as somewhat of a surprise considering George appears to be declining. But through the first two weeks, George has fit in with the Celtics seamlessly as the team has looked like a contender in the Eastern Conference. George is averaging 20.7 points, six rebounds and five assists. Coach Joe Mazzulla recently praised George's impact for being "beyond what's happening on the offensive end," pointing to George's leadership. -- Rhim Next games: vs. DAL (Nov. 4), @ SAC (Nov. 6), @ POR (Nov. 7), @ PHX (Nov. 9) Still working through kinks. San Antonio expected that, coming into the season, it would have to work through some hiccups with its new starting lineup, but Spurs coach Mitch Johnson is committed to seeing it through. And slowly, the group is starting to deliver on the promise Johnson saw when pondering whether to put them all together. Of course, Victor Wembanyama is at the center of it all, and San Antonio's dynamic guards are finding more ways to get him shots closer to the basket. Wembanyama currently leads the NBA in made alley-oops, averaging 3.8 per game, more than twice the average of any other player. -- Wright Next games: vs. IND (Nov. 4), vs. OKC (Nov. 6), @ TOR (Nov. 9) Kleiman "conviction" is confirmed. After last season's trade deadline, Grizzlies general manager Zach Kleiman expressed confidence in what was left in Memphis after jettisoning key players -- Desmond Bane the previous summer and later Jaren Jackson Jr. -- from a roster previously expected to contend for years to come. Kleiman moved the final player, Ja Morant, in June. But on that February day, Kleiman discussed his "conviction" in "pivoting to a younger build" that was "not going to be some drawn-out five-year process." Perhaps he was right, considering Memphis' 6-1 start behind young players such as Cameron Boozer and Cedric Coward taking on major roles alongside a resurgent Ty Jerome.-- Wright Next games: @ SAC (Nov. 4), vs. POR (Nov. 6), @ DET (Nov. 8), @ ATL (Nov. 9) Luka's on a heater It's hard to imagine a better start to the season for the Slovenian sharpshooter, leading the league in scoring with 38.3 points per game on percentage splits of 49.7/42.7/88.7. After he scored 42 in a rout of the Heat on Monday, Giannis Antetokounmpo wondered aloud whether Doncic wasn't just establishing himself as the best scorer in today's game, but rather the best to ever put the ball in the basket in the history of the game. Most encouraging for L.A., the points have come with wins. The Lakers are 6-2 out of the gates. -- Dave McMenamin Next games: @ PHX (Nov. 4), @ LAL (Nov. 6), vs. SA (Nov. 7), vs. OKC (Nov. 10) Rolling along without Ja. While critics of Portland's offseason trade for Morant questioned his fit in a crowded backcourt, it pays to have extra depth in the modern NBA. Countless teams are struggling to cope with early-season injuries to key players, but the Blazers have maintained their positive momentum despite losing Morant to a strained hamstring after only four games. Deni Avdija and Damian Lillard kept the offense humming throughout a convincing road win over Denver on Monday. Meanwhile, Scoot Henderson has stepped into Morant's starting spot to bolster Portland's perimeter defense, and veteran Jrue Holiday has thrived as a selfless sixth man. -- Ben Golliver Next games: @ OKC (Nov. 4), vs. PHI (Nov. 6), vs. NYK (Nov. 7), @ CHA (Nov. 9) Still figuring themselves out. The good news is Cleveland has more wins than losses; the bad news is the Cavaliers haven't looked that smooth in the process, with Peyton Watson in particular struggling to jell with his new squad. Cleveland has plenty of time to find its form, but the early returns are mixed rather than overwhelmingly positive. -- Zach Kram Next games: vs. CLE (Nov. 4), @ MEM (Nov. 6), vs. WAS (Nov. 7), @ POR (Nov. 10) Injuries are adding up.  The injuries to four All-Defensive players -- Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace, Chet Holmgren and Alex Caruso -- have robbed the Thunder of one of their offensive superpowers. The Thunder have averaged only 11.8 points off of turnovers in the past four games, which ranks third to last in the league during that span. By contrast, Oklahoma City led the NBA in points off of turnovers in each of the past three seasons. -- Tim MacMahon Next games: @ HOU (Nov. 4), @ NO (Nov. 6), vs. UTAH (Nov. 8) Come back soon, Ant. The Timberwolves are hanging tough without Anthony Edwards, who is expected to sit out two months after undergoing a knee procedure. Without their franchise guard, the Timberwolves struggled to sustain their newfound happy-go-lucky vibes during losses to the Warriors and Spurs. But Minnesota did take care of business against the Clippers and Bucks -- two projected bottom-dwellers -- to keep its head above water. Ayo Dosunmu, who signed a five-year, $112 million contract this summer, will get the chance to prove his worth while starting in place of Edwards. -- Golliver Next games: vs. MIA (Nov. 5), vs. ORL (Nov. 7), vs. NO (Nov. 9) Yaxel Lendeborg has arrived. The No. 11 pick in June's draft has already scored 26, 26, 31 and 37 points in his first two weeks in the NBA. His latest outburst, which included six 3s, came in a win over the LA Clippers in which Stephen Curry and Draymond Green rested. This Warriors team just followed an 0-3 start with a sudden five-game surge, and Curry, after the fifth straight win, was asked what changed. "Yax," Curry said. The Warriors didn't win five straight all of last season. The Warriors drafted a 24-year-old, 6-foot-10 power wing who has immediately looked like a top-30ish player in the NBA. "Changes everything," coach Steve Kerr said. -- Anthony Slater Next games: @ SA (Nov. 4), vs. UTAH (Nov. 6), vs. BKN (Nov. 8), vs. IND (Nov. 9) Flagg is taking off. Cooper Flagg's ascent to becoming an elite scorer hit a speed bump in Monday's loss to the previously winless Kings, when the 19-year-old went 3-of-19 from the field. Flagg is still averaging 25.2 points this season. The only players in NBA history to average that many points at age 20 or younger: LeBron James, Luka Doncic, Kevin Durant and Zion Williamson. -- MacMahon Next games: @ DEN (Nov. 4), @ MIL (Nov. 6), vs. MEM (Nov. 9) Life without Kawhi, again.  After reacquiring Leonard in a trade this offseason, the Raptors have already been forced to deal with the reality of Leonard: one of the league's best players who has been consistently sidelined because of left knee swelling. Still, the Raptors have remained afloat thanks to Scottie Barnes, who is ninth in steals per game (2.1) and 13th in scoring (24.4), and a historically suffocating defense that leads the league with 20.9 turnovers per game. -- Rhim Wednesday, Nov. 11
• Cavaliers-Knicks, 7 p.m. ET
• Warriors-Rockets, 9:30 p.m. ET Wednesday, Nov. 18
• Bucks-Heat, 7 p.m. ET
• Warriors-Mavericks, 9:30 p.m. ET Next games: vs. TOR (Nov. 4), @ IND (Nov. 7), @ HOU (Nov. 9) A lone bright spot. Among several problems that emerged for the Nuggets in last April's first-round flameout to the injured Minnesota Timberwolves, Jamal Murray's lack of production was perhaps the most destructive. He shot 35.7% in the series, 26.2% on 3s and petered out in a 12-point elimination Game 6, missing 13 of 17 shots. That memory appears flushed to open the season. Murray is one of the hottest scorers in the NBA, averaging 27.3 points and making more than 50% of his 3s. Even so, the Nuggets are a wobbly 3-3, with a remarkably average offense, considering they still have Nikola Jokic manning the middle. They led the NBA with a 121.2 offensive rating last season. They're currently 16th at 112.6. -- Slater Next games: vs. ATL (Nov. 4), @ ATL (Nov. 6), @ OKC (Nov. 7), @ DET (Nov. 9) The ADs look great. Anthony Davis has been Washington's best player, averaging 23.0 points and 9.1 rebounds, and AJ Dybantsa -- whose two initials are the same as the veteran big man's -- has averaged 19 points on 50% shooting in his first three games in the NBA. That's everything Washington could have wanted from the two No. 1 picks so far. -- Kram Next games: vs. CHI (Nov. 4), @ CLE (Nov. 7), vs. MIL (Nov. 10) The Mikal Bridges question. The curious case of Bridges continues to start the season, culminating in him playing only 16 minutes against the Nets on Monday night. It's a small sample size, but he's averaging career lows in scoring and efficiency, and even his 3-point attempts are down. The Knicks made a concerted effort to get him going, but it seemed futile. "He's just got to keep playing," Knicks coach Mike Brown said. "Everybody goes through those ups and downs throughout the course of the season, and obviously, it's the beginning of the season right now, so he's got to find his way. "When you're in a funk, you got to find one or two things to hold your hat on." -- Goodwill Next games: @ WAS (Nov. 4), vs. WAS (Nov. 6), vs. BKN (Nov. 7), vs. LAL (Nov. 9) Taking advantage of circumstances. The standings will show Atlanta winning games against Cleveland and Indiana in the past week. What won't appear is Cleveland playing in the second night of a back-to-back and Indiana having only six healthy players. The Pacers became the first team to have six players available this early in the season since the 1948 Boston Celtics. -- Bobby Marks Next games: @ LAC (Nov. 4), @ GS (Nov. 5), @ SAC (Nov. 8), @ UTAH (Nov. 10) No D, no chance. A team with Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo should not have the fourth-worst defense in the NBA. But through the first two weeks of the season, Miami has given up an average of 125 points in their five losses. In their loss to the Lakers on Monday, Miami gave up 138 points, its most this season. This was the 10th time in franchise history (and the second time this season) the Heat have given up at least 130 points. -- Marks Next games: @ BKN (Nov. 4), vs. BOS (Nov. 6), vs. CLE (Nov. 9) They need their guards. Coby White played 16 minutes in his first game of the season Monday while Kon Knueppel has yet to debut, and the Hornets' offense has suffered without that starting backcourt. Sion James (28% shooting, 22% on 3s) and Dennis Schroder (37% shooting, 18% on 3s) started in their absence but didn't do much to put pressure on opposing defenses. -- Kram Next games: @ PHX (Nov. 5), @ GS (Nov. 7), @ SAC (Nov. 10) No home-court identity. The two road wins against New York and Toronto proved that Orlando can compete with the top teams in the East. Playing at home is a different story. The Magic capped the second week of the regular season with home losses to Boston and Washington. They are now 0-4 and one of five teams without a home win. They trail only Milwaukee, Charlotte and Brooklyn with the worst point differential in home games. -- Marks ESPN Analytics has unveiled its new NBA Trade Lab, an interactive web app for fans to build, save and vote on mock trades. After a concerning 0-4 start, New Orleans' stunning overtime victory over previously unbeaten Memphis on Monday was its third straight win without guard Dejounte Murray (personal reasons). Though Pelicans coach Jamahl Mosley opened the season with an undersized starting backcourt featuring Murray and Jeremiah Fears, his team's offensive efficiency has improved by nearly 10 points during Murray's absence. Herbert Jones and Karlo Matkovic have added more size and versatility to the new-look starting lineup during the winning streak, leaving Mosley with some difficult decisions once Murray returns. -- Golliver Next games: @ MEM (Nov. 4), vs. DEN (Nov. 7), @ DAL (Nov. 9) Injury bug bites again. It wasn't bad enough that Tyrese Haliburton is out for at least two weeks because of a hamstring injury. Indiana's entire starting five sat out Monday's game, albeit the second night of a back-to-back, giving the Pacers visions of last season when injuries to Haliburton started a wave throughout the roster. Indiana will have to survive this early-season slog and hope for a throwback to two years ago. The Pacers were under .500 in mid-December before turning their season around in January with a run that carried them to the Finals. -- Jamal Collier Next games: vs. POR (Nov. 4), vs. ORL (Nov. 5), vs. HOU (Nov. 7), vs. SA (Nov. 9), vs. LAC (Nov. 10) Who's doing the rebounding? The Suns are 29th in the league in rebounds per game, securing only 39.6 boards a night. In related news, Phoenix is 27th in opponent's offensive rebounds allowed per game (14.2). Both are contributing to the Suns ranking dead last in defensive rating, allowing 124 points per 100 possessions. We knew the center position was a soft spot for this roster heading into the season, but it has been even worse than expected so far. -- McMenamin Next games: vs. MIA (Nov. 4), vs. NO (Nov. 8), @ PHX (Nov. 10) Six-game losing streak. After routing the Sacramento Kings by 25 points to start the season, the Clippers lost their next six straight by an average margin 12.7 points. Their offense has been hard to come by. Their leading scorer, Darius Garland, is averaging 20.1 points on 43.5% shooting, and their second-leading scorer, Rui Hachimura, is averaging 13.4 points on just 36.9% shooting. Maybe their next game against the Heat will be just what they need -- considering how rough the Heat's defense has been so far (27th in the league). -- McMenamin Next games: @ NO (Nov. 4), @ DAL (Nov. 6), @ MIN (Nov. 8), vs. MIA (Nov. 10) Lauri Markkanen's slow start. Utah needs Markkanen to return to his All-Star form. The 7-footer is averaging 16.5 points and shooting only 38.5% from the field, including 34.3% from 3-point range. It doesn't help that Markkanen is now dealing with a sprained right (shooting) wrist as he attempts to establish a rhythm. -- MacMahon Download the ESPN app and enable Shams Charania's news alerts to receive push notifications for the latest updates first. Opt in by tapping the alerts bell in the top right corner. For more information, click here. Beginning of a rebuild. This is what step one of a rebuild looks like. The Bulls knew they had a long way to go when their new front office arrived this summer, and the start of the season has confirmed as much. They have one win in their first seven games and haven't been super competitive against a tough schedule (they played Toronto with Kawhi Leonard, Boston twice, and will face the Knicks and Sixers for a second time later this week). Chicago ranks in the bottom five in both offensive and defensive efficiency and, outside of Caleb Wilson's strong start, not much has gone right so far. -- Collier Next games: @ BOS (Nov. 4), vs. TOR (Nov. 6), vs. BOS (Nov. 8), @ NYK (Nov. 10) Who survives the season? After trading their superstar over the summer, the Bucks have an ill-fitting roster that is clearly in transition. Milwaukee is looking for a new identity and the start of the season has not been encouraging with this many new players on the roster. So, how will Milwaukee continue to remake its roster going forward? What does the future hold for some Bucks veterans, including Myles Turner, Kyle Kuzma and Tyler Herro, who are not on the same timeline as some of the Bucks' other young players, namely No. 10 pick Brayden Burries? -- Collier Next games: vs. CHA (Nov. 4), @ ATL (Nov. 7), @ DAL (Nov. 8) Playing with good intentions.  That's about all you can say about the Nets at this point. They've held late leads, they've competed. At times, like Monday, Brooklyn gets a little scattered or too heavily dependent on Julius Randle to retrieve the team from the muck and it has a quicksand effect. But on the positive side, the Nets rank No. 3 in the NBA with nearly 40% of their scoring coming from 3-point range, and No. 7 in makes at 14.3 per game. -- Goodwill Next games: vs. LAL (Nov. 4), vs. SA (Nov. 6), vs. MIA (Nov. 8), vs. ORL (Nov. 10) The rookie isn't shy. Here are Darius Acuff Jr.'s shot attempts in his first seven NBA games: 24, 26, 23, 20, 26, 25, 21. Everyone assumed the rebuilding Kings would give their 19-year-old point guard the ultimate green light. Acuff has accepted, slamming down the gas pedal. His first four games were inefficient. His past three have been encouraging -- 35-of-72 overall plus a 14-assist effort. Acuff's most recent outing also led the previously 0-6 Kings to their first win. He had 25 points in Dallas and closed it out with a flurry, scoring seven in the last five minutes, including a dagger 3-pointer over Cooper Flagg. -- Slater

title: General Motors taps PHEV sedan segment with Buick Electra GS - CarNewsChina.com
content: General Motors is ready to launch the Buick Electra GS plug-in hybrid sedan in China. Built jointly with SAIC, it will compete with some high-volume models from BYD and Geely. The Electra GS is on time, as Buick’s deliveries declined by 20.4% Year-Over-Year in China, according to China EV DataTracker. The Buick Electra GS was exposed in China by the local Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) during the domestic homologation process. It is a large sedan with dimensions of 4979/1914/1495 mm and a wheelbase of 2,865 mm. For clarity, it is 149 mm longer than the BYD Qin L DM-i sedan, marketed in some overseas markets under the Seal 6 name. The car’s exterior styling adopts a closed front end with a sizeable trapeze-shaped air intake, U-shaped headlights, semi-hidden door handles, a sleek roofline, a single taillight unit, and a ducktail spoiler. This sedan has approach and departure angles of 13 and 14 degrees, respectively. It rides on 18- or 19-inch wheels (225/50 R18 or 234/45 R19). The Electra GS can be optionally equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR sensor. The curb weight lies between 1,780 and 1,890 kg. Its gross weight reaches 2,300 kg. The entry-level Buick Electra GS sedan comes standard with a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated 15FMC petrol-powered engine with a peak power output of 72 kW (97 hp). This ICE is manufactured by SAIC. The same ICE is used by the Roewe Jiayue 07 crossover, the Saic H5 (Shangjie H5), the Buick Electra E7 SUV, and other models. This engine is paired with a 165 kW (221 hp) electric motor. The car’s top speed is 190 km/h. It adopts two LFP battery pack variants from Zenergy and Rept Battero. A more powerful variant of the Buick Electra GS has a 1.5-liter turbocharged LD3 engine with a peak power output of 115 kW (154 hp). The same engine is used by the Buick Electra L7 sedan, the Buick GL8 PHEV minivan, and other cars. This ICE also works in pairs with a 165 kW (221 hp) electric motor. The top-trim Electra GS has a top speed of 190 km/h and a Zenergy-made LFP battery. It seems that the entry-level Buick Electra GS sedan will rival the mentioned BYD Qin L DM-i sedan. The latter model offers a combination of a 1.5-liter engine for 74 kW (99 hp) and an electric motor with a peak power output of 160 kW (215 hp). BYD delivered 70,740 units of this sedan to customers in China from January to September 2026, according to China EV DataTracker. The Electra GS is expected to cost more than 100,000 yuan (14,970 USD) domestically.
